items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

items.originalTitle: The Far Right Wants to Kill Wolves Whenever and However They Please
items.author: The Intercept Briefing
items.title: The Far Right Wants to Kill Wolves Whenever and However They Please
items.summary: The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the 1990s is one of the most celebrated conservation comeback stories in history, thanks to the Endangered Species Act. Recently, however, wolves became a political football in a time of shifting politics in Montana. “It’s a barometer. What somebody feels about wolves might tell you what they feel about many other aspects of American political life,” says investigative journalist Ryan Devereaux. This week on The Intercept Briefing, senior editor Ali Gharib and Devereaux discuss the reporting in his new book, “ The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West ,” which documents how a 2021–2022 hunt became one of the deadliest assaults on Yellowstone’s wolves since the animals were completely wiped out around 100 years ago. “These were groups who gathered around the idea that reintroduction was not only a mistake, but that extirpation was correct and that we should return to the days of a wolf-free West,” says Devereaux. The successful passage of environmental protections in the ’70s had “also spawned a counterrevolution,” he adds. In Donald Trump’s second presidential term, many of those same anti-Endangered Species Act and anti-federal regulation figures now hold powerful positions in the agencies tasked with protecting wildlife and public lands. “A lot of what they planned to do was laid out in Project 2025, the planning document that laid out the blueprint for what Trump 2.0 would look like,” notes Devereaux. “In fact, if you go back and read the Department of Interior section of that document, you’ll see that the reintroduction of wolves under the Clinton administration is held up as the shining example of the way in which a network of liberals and environmentalists have ruined the West and the federal government has overstepped its bounds.” For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts. Transcript Ali Gharib: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing. I’m Ali Gharib, a senior editor at The Intercept. Today on The Briefing, we’re going to be talking about — drum roll — politics. But it’s a different type of politics than we’ve discussed here before. It’s the politics of wolves in the lower 48 states. A book on this very subject, “The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West,” recently came out from Avid Reader Press. Its author, Ryan Devereaux, will be joining us to talk about ground zero in the political war over wolves: Yellowstone National Park. Wolves were reintroduced into the park in the 1990s in what’s largely considered to be the greatest conservation success in history. But they became a political football as their presence was assailed, often with deadly violence by the far right. The 2021–2022 hunt itself was the deadliest assault on wolves around Yellowstone National Park since the animals were completely wiped out around 100 years ago. Some 25 Yellowstone wolves were killed , about a fifth of the park’s population, with an entire pack wiped out completely. Hunting is illegal in national parks, of course, so most of this hunting came right along the edge of the park in the public land surrounding it. Related Was Yellowstone’s Deadliest Wolf Hunt in 100 Years an Inside Job? The investigative story that gave rise to Ryan’s book was published by The Intercept in 2022, the year the hunt concluded. The article revealed that a park ranger had shot and killed the last wolf taken in the hunt himself, right at the knife’s edge by mere minutes of the end of the official hunt. In The Intercept article, Ryan also revealed a major probe by the Park Service’s internal investigative wing into this kill. The investigative report, though, was largely redacted. Since that article was published in 2022, Ryan and The Intercept won a lawsuit to release much of the file. The book is chock-full of new, never-before-seen material on the hunt, on the ranger’s kill. Fascinating stuff. I couldn’t recommend this book more highly. It’s informative, it’s exciting, and like all great journalism, it tells the gripping story of this hunt, which illuminates much larger truths about the world we’re living in today. Ryan was a longtime investigative reporter at The Intercept , but today he’s doing his work at ProPublica , where you can read his latest material as it comes out. Ryan, welcome to the Intercept Briefing. Ryan Devereaux: Thanks so much for having me. AG: Let’s get right to it, Ryan. As we’ve talked about before, and as you’ve written, this is really a story that’s as old as all the myths about the big bad wolf that Europeans brought with them to what would later become known as the Americas. But the episode of wolf history in the U.S. that you write about really starts to kick into high gear in the 1990s, when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone Park. Can you tell us about why there were no wolves in the park and just touch on the program about how to get them back? RD: The story is a long one, but I’ll try to keep it brief. When Europeans arrived here in North America, they brought with them a lot of cultural, spiritual, and religious baggage from the Old World relating to wilderness, and this idea that wilderness was a kind of space that needed to be tamed, conquered, and made productive. And to do that required moving out of the way the Native folks that they encountered when they got here, as well as much of the native wildlife, especially predators and wolves in particular — having featured prominently in the Bible and lots of European mythology as a symbol of evil and Satan — were right at the top of the list for extirpation. As the settlers marched West, they wiped out wolves wherever they found them. But the system was sort of ad hoc up until the early 1900s, when the federal government got involved and undertook a massive targeted killing program across the Lower 48 that resulted in extirpation by the 1920s and 1930s, including in Yellowstone National Park. As this was unfolding, new understandings of the role that species play vis-a-vis one another in ecosystems was beginning to flourish. A new field of ecology was being born. By the 1960s, Americans were starting to have much different understandings of the roles that predators played in ecosystems. By the 1970s, you had the environmental movement in full swing, and the passage of a whole bunch of new critical federal laws, including the Endangered Species Act . The ESA is what paved the way to wolf reintroduction in the 1990s. So it happened in January 1995 in Yellowstone National Park, as well as the wilderness of Idaho just to the west. Dozens of wolves captured in the Canadian Rockies were transported to Yellowstone National Park. They were welcomed with schoolchildren on the side of the road there in Gardiner, which is the northern gateway to the park in southwest Montana, but also a ton of controversy. This was unfolding in the mid-1990s. 1994, the year before, was the Republican revolution, the first time that the GOP had taken control of Congress in decades, a flowering of culture-war battles in American political life. And this issue — this initiative — in the West became the touchstone symbol of the growing divide between segments of the population in the Northern Rockies. AG: That was the backdrop of the changes in politics, sort of proto-MAGA era, right? These changes in Montana really came to fruition in this century, when Montana went from being a purple state with eclectic politics to being much more in the kind of MAGA evangelical stronghold world, which led to the rise of one of the central figures of your book, the governor of Montana: Greg Gianforte . Can you talk about, briefly, the shifts in Montana politics and how Gianforte came to power? RD: Yeah, it’s a fascinating story, and in many ways, Gianforte is representative of the changes that Montana in particular has experienced over the last three decades. He arrived in the state in 1995, in fact, the same year that the wolves were reintroduced — and he came amid this larger wave of new arrivals to the region. They’re sometimes known as the “modem cowboys.” These were well-to-do individuals who realized that they could do their jobs free from the coastal environments that they had historically lived in because technology was allowing them to do so. Gianforte has spoken about this specifically. He was a tech executive who made his money in software development in the Bozeman area. He was extraordinarily successful in doing so, and he came in at this time in the late ’90s, into the 2000s, into the 2010s, making a lot of money in tech, and then deciding he wanted to move into politics after he sold his company. He spent a lot of his own fortune in attempts to run for office as a governor and in Congress. Some folks might remember a few years back, Gianforte first broke into the national spotlight when he choke-slammed a journalist who had asked him a question about healthcare — and then he won his special congressional race the next day. This was just after Trump had come in the first time. [Gianforte] manages to successfully run for governor in the Covid, racial justice protest summer of 2020 , and he takes office in 2021. What that does is change a tradition of ticket-splitting that had held firm in Montana for about a decade and a half. The state hadn’t had a Republican governor since the Bush administration. What that allows, with respect to wolves, is Republican lawmakers who had been fighting ever since the 1995 reintroduction for a much heavier hand in wolf management to put forward a number of bills that would really aim to slash the state’s wolf population dramatically and see them green-lit by the governor. That’s essentially what happens over the next several months in the 2021 legislative session. There’s also an incident involving Gianforte’s own interest in hunting a wolf that kicks off that year — I can talk about that as well, if it sounds interesting. But that’s the backdrop to how all of this began to unfold in 2021 and led to the hunt that I write about in the book. AG: Yeah, Ryan, I’d love to hear you talk about the incident involving Gianforte. It was just within a month of him taking office, right? RD: That’s right. The governor, shortly after taking office, killed a Yellowstone wolf , a radio-collared Yellowstone wolf. Not only that, he killed a Yellowstone wolf on the property of a campaign donor who owns a mega-ranch in the Paradise Valley, which is this extraordinary valley that runs from around the Livingston area down to the park’s gateway, the sort of setting of “Yellowstone,” the TV show. Word spread in the state that this had happened. The governor had killed a wolf. The state’s fish and wildlife department – whenever somebody kills a wolf legally, they have to register with the state. Game wardens have to check out the situation, sign off on it. Gianforte called his wolf in. And I write about the head of wildlife law enforcement for the state realizing it’s going to be up to him to check in the governor’s wolf kill. There is an alleged attempt by the governor and his partner in the wolf hunt to shift responsibility for the kill from the governor to his hunting partner. It was discovered during the course of looking into things by the fish and wildlife department that the governor had failed to take a requisite trapping course prior to killing this wolf. The governor and his buddy have insisted that everything that they did was aboveboard here, but this killing of a park wolf — a radio-collared wolf, no less — right at the beginning of his tenure, set the tone in many ways for what was to follow. The alleged attempt at a cover-up didn’t come out until much, much later. I had discovered it early in the course of my reporting. But yeah, that was the big opening event. Related Montana Judge Won’t Halt Gov. Greg Gianforte’s Aggressive Wolf Hunt After that you saw Gianforte sign a number of bills with respect to wolves that would allow a whole host of new measures, including night hunting, hunting over bait, hunting with night-vision goggles, and most critically, as it pertains to this story, the elimination of hunting quotas north of Yellowstone. There’s two districts north of the park. The quotas before the governor came in were one in each district, and after he took office and after this legislative session, there were no limits whatsoever. AG: This is crucial to your book, and one of the reasons I love this Gianforte story is that there were these meager regulations, and he, according to the citation that he got, wasn’t even able to follow them for this wolf that he trapped himself in early 2021. By late 2021, the entire ground has shifted, and even these regulations that he wasn’t able to follow are gone, and everything has been undone. There are these proposals that come from the laws that Gianforte signed, and they have to pass through the Fish, Wildlife, and Parks Commission in Montana, which is the regulatory body for protecting wildlife in the state, including administering all the hunts. This is not a model unique to Montana, but the bureaucracy of FWP is overseen by a commission. The commission is assigned by the governor. Related Lauren Boebert Waved Around Pictures of Dead Babies in Her Call to Gut the Endangered Species Act But FWP itself was storied, not only in the region, but across the country for being extremely rigorously based in science in Montana. That was something that just in the span of a very short time from Gianforte taking office was completely turned on its head, and instead we had a very anti-science perspective that we’re still seeing with regard to the politics of endangered species in the country. But can you talk about FWP and how, and the options they were presented with, and how Gianforte’s FWP went whole hog on wiping out regulations? RD: The story with wildlife governance, like so many bureaucracies, it has a deep history. In the West, it has something to do with our settler expansionist roots. As settlers moved West, there’s this mass killing of wildlife along the way. It’s not just wolves, and it’s not just bison killing, which were killed by the tens of millions. As settlers put down roots in what would become these western states, they tore into local game populations. They created game markets where the meat and hides of wildlife were sold by the ton. It became evident fairly early on in the late 1800s, early 1900s, that this was not sustainable . Wildlife was starting to disappear, including in states like Montana. Nascent government bodies were formed to address this issue. “These [fish and wildlife] commissions tend to be populated by, often, folks who’ve contributed to the governor who appoints them.” States created state fish and wildlife departments, and as you described, they created these game commissions, these fish and wildlife commissions, to set the rules and regulations for those departments. The model’s pretty much the same across the country, and especially in the West. These commissions tend to be populated by, often, folks who’ve contributed to the governor who appoints them. In many cases, they serve at will. Across the country, the qualifications for serving on these commissions vary, but it’s actually somewhat rare for commissioners to be required to have any background in wildlife management, biology, and science. Typically, historically, they’ve represented industries that have a stake in wildlife. That’s big game hunting industries, livestock production, that sort of thing. That trend has remained a constant throughout history and throughout the West. Montana as a state and its Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks —everybody knows as FWP — as you described, became a model in the mid-1900s of progressive, science-based wildlife management. Because the new arrivals to the state dug so deep into the wildlife populations, the fish and wildlife department took it upon themselves to start reintroducing different types of huntable species. They were pretty successful with this, actually quite successful. They were among the first departments in the country to require that their biologists have a master’s degree . “Montana as a state and its Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Parks … became a model in the mid-1900s of progressive, science-based wildlife management.” It was the kind of place where if you were interested in doing high-quality scientific wildlife management work at the state level, Montana was the place to be. You had this incredible range of species, and you had a department that was serious about its science. The folks who went to work there prided themselves, especially the biologists, on their ability to be self-sufficient, to be in their communities, to know what their communities needed, what they wanted, and what they expected from wildlife management policy in their area. I’m getting all of this based on a number of people who I interviewed who devoted their careers to this department, and what they described as a change — the political change — in Montana were new rules that prohibited them from speaking directly to their commissioner about policy decisions. A feeling that they were being muzzled and that their actual views on what policies should look like weren’t being heard, and that those decisions were instead being made in Helena, the state capital, by lawmakers. This was particularly pronounced and particularly evident in the way that the policy was formed around wolf management in 2021. You had lawmakers, mostly from Northwest Montana, which is a different scene ecologically, socially, politically, economically than Southwest Montana, creating wolf policy for the entire state based on arguments that were frankly pretty flimsy. Related A Biologist Fought to Remove Grizzlies From the Endangered Species List — Until Montana Republicans Changed His Mind Those arguments were turned into law, which were turned into policy that the department had to implement. And this was deeply frustrating for career biologists who worked in some of these places in Southwest Montana, where the issues with wolves, livestock, elk were different than they are in Northwest Montana. It was a really deep and, in many cases, profoundly upsetting experience for a lot of career biologists in the state. “You had lawmakers, mostly from Northwest Montana, which is a different scene ecologically, socially, politically, economically than Southwest Montana, creating wolf policy for the entire state based on arguments that were frankly pretty flimsy.” AG: OK, so Ryan, the climactic action of this bureaucratic wrangling to deregulate wolf hunts happens with a vote by the Fish and Wildlife Commission. On a personal note, Ryan and I have spent a lot of time in Southwest Montana and especially camping in Yellowstone Park. And on the day this vote was held, we were actually in a parking lot on Slough Creek, this area northwest of the park, the Lamar Valley, known as one of the best wildlife spotting places in the country, if not the world, with a Ford van that wouldn’t start — and a bunch of wolves running around. This wasn’t like spotting scopes from 300 yards. This was like, we were looking at them with our naked eye, crossing rivers. It was really a remarkable thing. What had happened that summer was that one bison had gored another to death, and the park rangers had moved the carcass a little bit further from the road, but still close enough that it was within full view, and it just became — what longtime wolf observers have said — was the best wolf viewing time in their lifetimes. Incredible numbers of people got to see these wolves. We were camping in the area. We heard them howl at night. We didn’t even care that the van wouldn’t start. We were just sitting there enjoying the sights and sounds of these wolves, and it was really a remarkable scene. On that same day we were sitting there, the FWP commission was voting from three different options of what would be allowed — the extreme methods that would be allowed, less extreme to more extreme of wolf hunting. Can you talk briefly about that vote and what the different categories of regulations were? RD: I’ll just add that was an extraordinary moment in time to be in the park. The park’s largest and most famous wolf pack. It was known as Junction Butte . They had 18 pups survive from the previous season, which is basically unheard of. So the pack was going into this season with big numbers. Just the year before, the biologists involved in the reintroduction had written a book collectively marking the 25th anniversary of the reintroduction and all its achievements. They wrote about it describing how the story of reintroduction, the story of how the United States government went from a policy of wolf eradication to wolf reintroduction , was a story of a change of heart. It was a book that had this tone of accomplishment and a joy and a hard-won victory. All of that was about to come crashing down with the vote that you were describing. “The story of how the U.S. government went from a policy of wolf eradication to wolf reintroduction was a story of a change of heart.” Over the summer, the Fish and Wildlife Commission had put forward a slew of different ideas for how the hunt that winter could take shape. There were these hearings that were held, and members of the public came out in huge numbers. Wolf hearings in general bring out a lot of people. But there was a ton of public pushback against this direction that the commission was clearly drifting, which was toward extraordinarily heavy-handed wolf management. On the day in question, there were, like you said, three options that were put forward — basically a light, medium, and hard wolf management regime. Biologists in the department felt like, after many years of conflict, they had settled on a suite of policies that was maintaining a steady population. People who wanted to hunt wolves were getting the opportunity to do so; a lot of the rancor over this issue had quieted down. So their light option was basically keep the status quo. We’ll make a couple tweaks to satisfy new laws that were passed during the legislative session that we have to make because they’re legally required, but by and large we’ll stay the course. The medium option incorporated, as you might expect, some of the heavy-handed measures that I described before that lawmakers were interested in implementing. The heavy option was everything: Bring all of the tools to bear in an effort to reduce the state’s population to the greatest degree possible. It was a heated hearing. The hard-liner, anti-wolf faction was roundly outnumbered by a whole host of local Montanans, including hunters, people from around the country who didn’t think that this was scientific and had no basis or justification based on the state’s own analysis. Because a lot of these measures were justified on the basis of the claim that wolves were decimating the state’s elk population, when in fact there were more elk in Montana than there were at the time of reintroduction in 1995. According to some population biologists, there were probably as many there as were there in the past couple centuries. In Paradise Valley, just north of the park, ranchers consistently complained about there being too many elk and the problems that that created for their line of work. In fact, even Gianforte, when he was running for governor, described how the overabundance of elk in southwest Montana was a problem. So the core basis for the argument for going as hard as possible, it didn’t have a leg to stand on, and yet at the end of the day, the commission green-lit the most heavy-handed suite of wolf management options possible. That included all of the measures I described, as well as the elimination of quotas on Yellowstone’s border. What that signaled to the relatively small but extraordinarily motivated cohort of hunters and trappers who live around the park was that it was “go time” and an opportunity that they had been waiting for a quarter century was finally there, an opportunity to punch back the wolf population in the park and everything it represented. [Break] AG: This is really crucial to your story, because this is part of the 2021 hunt. It was this extraordinary number of wolves killed, and much of it happened in the two districts north of the park, and half of those wolves that were killed were taken by just four people who are pretty known figures in this area as being extreme anti-wolf ideologues. Which brings us to the titular hunt of your book. It’s an extraordinary moment, and it’s gone from this day you and I were watching the greatest wolf-watching experience, the culmination of 25 years of reintroduction — wolves just jaunting around in plain view of tourists like us in the park — to the winter of 2021–2022. Can you just run down some of the devastating consequences for Yellowstone wolves of the hunt itself? RD: To your point about the relatively small number of people who were participating in the hunt, it’s absolutely true. This is a small-town community, Gardiner, Montana, an unincorporated community. Everybody knows everybody, and to a large degree, everybody knows what everybody else feels about wolves. It’s a barometer. What somebody feels about wolves might tell you what they feel about many other aspects of American political life. The most motivated of these guys, they didn’t keep their feelings about the reintroduction secret. When Gianforte was running for governor, one of these guys posted photos of dead wolves in front of a “Make America Great Again” yard sign. On social media, their accounts abounded with photos of dead wolves; it was often couched in the language of saving elk and basically sticking it to the libs. But while it was a rather small number of people doing the actual killing, the way that they would do it is cluster around a couple of key wildlife migration corridors that empty out of the park. Same places where hunters hunt other species, wolves follow their prey species through these corridors into the Gardiner area. “Their accounts abounded with photos of dead wolves; it was often couched in the language of saving elk and basically sticking it to the libs.” These are wide-open territories. These are wolves that could grow up in a national park. It’s not an area where you have to engage in some multi-day backpacking journey to get yourself a wolf. They’re coming out in the open, and they don’t know any better around people. These areas, one known as Beattie Gulch and another called Deckard Flats, became shooting galleries for wolves. But to the point about, a small number of people engaging in that kind of activity, that is true. At the same time, however, it didn’t take a lot of research on my part to find online communities that were fairly substantial in number really rooting for this hunt to be absolutely as deadly as possible. Social media groups devoted to wolf hunting and trapping, not because they saw it in the way that some hunting groups devoted to other species like revel in the challenge or procuring their own meat for the winter. These were groups who gathered around the idea that reintroduction was not only a mistake, but that extirpation was correct and that we should return to the days of a wolf-free West. When Gianforte and the Republicans in Montana gave the green light to this hunt, those groups were rejoicing and demanding the highest body count possible, and it started right away. Within the first week of the hunt, there were two pups and a yearling taken from that Junction Butte pack that you and I had watched right north of the park. From there, it took a little time to get going through the fall, but by the winter, the rate of killing was starting to pick up. By the end of the year the season had already surpassed the previous deadliest season, in which I believe around a dozen wolves were killed, and there were still many weeks to go. “These were groups who gathered around the idea that reintroduction was not only a mistake, but that extirpation was correct and that we should return to the days of a wolf-free West.” AG: I edited the original long investigation that you did for The Intercept . You got to talk about the park ranger who was involved in the hunt and what happened there. This was Beattie Gulch, this is the area right outside the park. The proximity plays a crucial role here in the last, literally, the last moments right at the edge of the legal territory of the wolf hunt and the subsequent National Park Service investigation. Can you give us a quick rundown with leaving a little bit to pique readers’ interests of what happened with the park ranger? RD: As this hunt was escalating and reaching its crescendo, there was one commissioner on Montana’s Fish and Wildlife Commission who was a holdover from the previous governorship, and he was responsible for the region that includes Yellowstone in southwest Montana. He actually called for an emergency meeting about the extraordinarily high death toll resulting from the hunt and said, “We got to call this off.” Long story short, that effort was ultimately unsuccessful. And within a couple days, the biologists at Yellowstone National Park, the wolf team, had gotten word that a radio-collared wolf had been reported killed in the Beattie Gulch area. That was not unusual. That’s how things had been going the entire season. But without giving away too much, there were some unusual elements to this situation. The wolf’s collar had indicated that it was inside the park when legal hunting hours in Montana closed that night. The route that the collar took after the hunting hours closed was somewhat suspect. What ultimately came to light was that the wolf was taken by a veteran Yellowstone Park law enforcement ranger, perhaps the most veteran working in the park at the time, a ranger who had been in Yellowstone since 10 years before the wolves were reintroduced and was actually among a cohort of rangers who were assigned to protect the wolves when they were returned to their to the park. This set off a series of events, which included a serious investigation executed by what is effectively the National Park Service’s equivalent to an FBI unit. What they call a “Tier 1” investigation was started, to look into the possibility that this ranger had been sharing the location of wolves to hunters outside of the park throughout the season, and also into the specifics of his hunt specifically. I managed to obtain a large investigative file through a public records request when I first got this tip, and it confirmed the existence of the investigation. It included a couple maps, including where the wolf was taken, and confirmed that a Yellowstone ranger was the subject of the investigation. “Everything else in this nearly 300-page report was blacked out, redacted, as though it were some national security file. … To see that level of secrecy around a wolf kill was surprising.” But everything else in this nearly 300-page report was blacked out, redacted, as though it were some national security file. That was unusual to me, having reported in those contexts before , to see that level of secrecy around a wolf kill was surprising, to say the least. I managed to speak to this ranger at length in a couple of interviews, and he spoke to me on the record in detail about what happened that night — the night of his kill. He denied that the wolf was taken after hunting hours, and in fact the state game warden confirmed his account, recording his hunt as having been completed just a few minutes before the hunting hours closed. The wolf was definitely taken outside of the park. I later visited the location where the wolf was killed. It was right on the border, but nobody, as the ranger told me, knew that border better than he did. He was never charged with a crime. He retired as this investigation was running its course, but as this news started to percolate around Gardiner, among people in the know, especially in the park, especially among his now former colleagues [were] deeply, deeply upset. Because this wasn’t the first or second wolf killed in a normal hunting season. It was the 25th in the deadliest season that the park had ever seen, in a season that had pit Gianforte, the governor, against the manager, the superintendent of Yellowstone. It was a decision made consciously. The ranger told me, look, I purchased a hunting license just like anybody else, I took advantage of an opportunity that was there. Wolves should be managed like any other species, and I chose to exercise my right to do so. But to folks inside the park, it felt like something deeper and more painful. We published this investigation in the summer of 2022, and I still had a ton of questions about what was under those redactions, how truthful the ranger had been with me, how exactly was this investigation experienced by people who were working inside the park at the time. Through collaboration with The Intercept, we filed a federal lawsuit seeking to repeal — remove some of those redactions — and we had a lot of success with that. I was able to unearth some new details that I’ll leave for readers to check out. But it added a lot more complexity and layers to this whole episode. AG: We should shout out our attorney here, David Bralow, who helped out on that lawsuit, and I know is super, super proud of getting that stuff out there. It just adds, from the story we did to the section of your book that deals with this particular part of the wolf hunt, it’s just the rich detail there, it really reads like a thriller. It’s a lot of fun to pick it up, even having worked on the initial story. That was the hunt. It was devastating. It was a sign of these changing politics. There’s a reason it’s the title of your book, right? It’s really at the heart of telling this story. But this is a much, much broader story. It’s a broader story about politics, and it’s a broader story about wildlife management. I have two questions to wrap up here that are throwing the story forward a little bit. What’s happened since then with the wolf hunt? That was the 2021–2022 hunting season. What’s going on with wolves in Montana and Yellowstone; what’s the latest with the regulations? Has there been a come-to-Jesus moment? Is the course being stayed? Then the other question — and this is a huge question — but this is one piece of a much larger battle about the roadless rule, about building new roads in Forest Service public lands, and about wilderness areas, about extractive industries in these public lands, about hunting, grazing, selling off public lands. The whole thing. Related Grizzly Bear Poachers Flout the Endangered Species Act — and Get Away With It Public lands and wild spaces and wildlife are all being assailed from so many different directions. This is to say nothing of the dismantling of the Endangered Species Act and other large predators like the grizzly bear and what’s happening with their listing under the Endangered Species Act. What set all this off was the delisting of the wolf as populations recovered from having the highest levels of protection from the ESA. Now we’re facing that with grizzly bears as well. Can you put this in the context of the broader fights happening over public land right now in the U.S.? RD: To answer the first question, what’s going on with wolves in Yellowstone National Park and what happened with rules and regulations after the hunt. There are a number of organizations, companies, individuals whose livelihoods are built around the wolf population that recovered post-1995 in Yellowstone. There’s an enormous wildlife watching industry that has cropped up and in some ways has supplanted or is supplanting the guided hunting industry that dominated that region when Yellowstone’s northern range was free of its native predators. After the hunt, a coalition was formed of wildlife watching groups, hospitality industry folks, even some outfitters who aren’t hardcore anti-wolf to say that we care about this ecosystem being intact. It affects our livelihoods. Their group, Wild Livelihoods, commissioned a study to look at just how much wolf watching contributes to the local economy, and the estimate that they found was somewhere in the ballpark of $82 million a year going to the local economy. There is some trepidation among these folks in terms of using an economic argument to rein in overly aggressive wolf management policy. These folks would rather be making an argument for the intrinsic value of these animals, but they also recognize that they live in a capitalist society, and money does talk. They took these arguments to the Fish and Wildlife Commission for the following season, and they were able to reinstate quotas north of the park. They were not the 1 in 1 — the low 1 in 1 — quotas that existed prior to Gianforte’s election, but there was some level of restriction implemented. However, everything else, all of the other measures, the night hunting, snaring, baiting, all of that stuff still remained in place. Related Secretive Federal Agency’s Days of Killing Pets With Poison Bombs May Finally Be Ending Across the rest of Montana, very little change. Year to year, legislative session to legislative session, the same actors who advocated for this ultra-aggressive hunt are showing up year after year in Helena, putting forward new bills. They would like to see wolves across the state classified as a predator, which in the sort of parlance of wildlife governance has nothing to do with what an animal eats. It has everything to do with the kind of protections that they receive under the law. An animal classified as a predator, like a coyote, can be killed any time of year in any number by any means necessary . They’re also fighting for a yearlong hunting season, which would allow for the hunting of pups — which is critical if you want to really make a dent in a wildlife population. It’s already happening in Idaho . As for the wolves themselves, in the park’s boundaries, there was a major disease outbreak over the past year that took out a big chunk of the population. So in terms of the number of wolves on the ground, it’s significantly lower than it was that year that you and I visited. So it’s a complicated story. Some wins for wolf advocates, some losses. As for the bigger picture, one of the core threads that I chart in this book is how the 1970s environmental movement led to this slew of new federal environmental laws, the Endangered Species Act kind of being the shining example, and the shining example of Endangered Species Act initiatives being the reintroduction of wolves in the West. But that moment in history also spawned a counterrevolution. It’s known as the Sagebrush Rebellion . But it also goes deeper than the Sagebrush rebels, where there was a coalescence of industry actors and conservatives in the West who saw these new federal regulations as constraining the power that they had over the region for generations. And they’ve been organizing and fighting back ever since. [In] the 1980s, under the Reagan administration, they had the upper hand for quite a while. There’s a reason it took 20 years after the ESA was passed, after initial wolf recovery plans were kicked around, that it took before they were actually reintroduced. There was an intense fight, and a lot of the figures who have been deeply involved in that anti-federal regulation, anti-ESA world have been vying to return to power ever since. With Trump’s second election, a number of those actors have assumed powerful positions in the federal government, the Department of Interior, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Related Trump “National Police Force” Built on ICE Partnerships With Local Agencies Like… Wildlife Commissions? A lot of what they planned to do was laid out in Project 2025, the planning document that laid out the blueprint for what Trump 2.0 would look like. In fact, if you go back and read the Department of Interior section of that document, you’ll see that the reintroduction of wolves under the Clinton administration is held up as the shining example of the way in which a network of liberals and environmentalists have ruined the West and the federal government has overstepped its bounds. It is held up as an example of the kind of overreach that needs to be reined in. What we’ve seen since Trump has returned to office is a kind of attack on this whole suite of laws passed in the 1970s, the ESA right at the top of that list. This law, which has historically passed with huge bipartisan support and has historically remained one of the more popular environmental laws in the country, is under threat like never before. You see initiatives and species that are associated with that law also under threat, and that is certainly the case with wolves, also the case with public lands. All of these things are very interrelated, especially in the West. AG: Ryan, we’re going to leave it there. Thanks for joining us. This is such a huge and important story for the world we’re living in. Everybody should go out and read this book. I loved it so much. It’s called “ The Hunt: A True Story of Resurrection and Retribution in the West .” It’s available everywhere, but you should probably go pick it up at your local bookseller. Thanks again, Ryan, for speaking to us and joining us on The Intercept Briefing. RD: Thanks so much for having me. AG: That does it for this episode. This episode was produced by Laura Flynn. Ben Muessig is our editor-in-chief. Maia Hibbett is the managing editor of The Intercept. Chelsea B. Coombs is our social media producer. Nara Shin is the copy editor. Will Stanton mixed the show, and the legal review, as always, is done by David Bralow. Slipstream provided our theme music. The show and reporting at The Intercept doesn’t exist without you, our listeners and readers. Your donation, no matter the amount, makes a huge difference for us. Keep our investigations free and fearless at theintercept.com/join . If you haven’t already, please subscribe to The Intercept Briefing wherever you listen to your pods, and please leave us a rating or a review. It really helps other listeners find us. Let us know what you think of this episode, or if you’d like to send us a general message, you can email us at podcast@theintercept.com . Someone will read it. Until next time, I’m Ali Gharib. Thanks for listening. The post The Far Right Wants to Kill Wolves Whenever and However They Please appeared first on The Intercept .

items.originalTitle: The good news about homelessness comes with a catch
items.author: Rachel Cohen Booth
items.title: The good news about homelessness comes with a catch
items.summary: Tents belonging to homeless people are set up between Schleusenkrug and Bahnhof Zoo in the Charlottenburg neighborhood, next to an S-Bahn line. | Marion van der Kraats/picture alliance via Getty Images On a cold winter night in January, social workers and volunteers in towns and cities across the country fanned out to look for anyone living without shelter — on benches, on trains, on steps outside churches, in tents below underpasses. The goal of this national ritual is to get an accurate estimate of how many homeless people are out there each year. Combined with additional data on people staying in shelters, it’s the basis for the US Department of Housing and Urban Development’s Point-in-Time Count , the federal government’s benchmark number. And there’s some good news in this year’s count, which HUD preliminarily released this month. Trump administration officials announced that 698,425 people were homeless on a single night in January, down 6.3 percent from a year earlier. HUD released the number ahead of its full annual report to Congress, but if it holds, it would be the largest one-year drop since national counts began in 2007. A separate analysis commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness (NAEH) estimated a similar 6.7 percent decline. Key takeaways Preliminary federal data shows homelessness down 6.3 percent, which would be the biggest one-year drop since 2007. Fewer migrants, slower rent growth, and local programs all likely helped, but no one knows how much. Chronic homelessness, the focus of Trump’s overhaul, barely changed. It marks the second straight year the national homelessness count has fallen. Homelessness had climbed by about a third between 2022 and 2024, hitting a record of about 771,000 people in 2024, then fell to 745,652 in 2025 . But there are also competing stories as to what’s behind the positive trend, as well as the more persistent trouble spots, that pit the White House and housing advocates against each other, with each favoring very different policy approaches. The stakes are high for them to get it right — while homelessness is declining nationwide, the number of people who have been homeless for prolonged periods and often face especially dire challenges has remained stubbornly high. Why are there fewer homeless people in 2026? The Trump administration and homeless advocates point to different explanations to account for the recent drop. “President Trump’s actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner told Vox in a statement. Both sides agree that the rapidly decreasing number of newly arrived migrants is a part of the story. The asylum-seekers who crowded into shelters in Boston, Chicago, Denver, and New York City in 2023 and 2024 are mostly gone now, and economists at the University of Chicago and Dartmouth estimated that asylum-seekers accounted for about 60 percent of the jump in shelter counts during those two years. Every expert I talked to said their departure explains at least part of this year’s national drop. Slower rent growth, a stronger job market, and communities recovering from disasters like Hurricane Helene and the Maui fires likely helped, too. There are some limits to the data. While fewer people are homeless than a year ago, per the new Point-in-Time survey, HUD’s annual count notoriously excludes many people without a stable home , like those doubled up with relatives or living week to week in motels. But the heart of the dispute between the White House and advocates are chronically homeless people, meaning those who’ve been homeless for at least a year, or repeatedly over a three-year period, and have a serious mental illness or addiction. Their numbers seem to have barely budged in the NAEH’s review. Turner blames “failed Housing First policies” — the approach of giving people permanent housing without first requiring them to get sober or enter treatment — for keeping homelessness so high in the US. In this telling, tough love is needed to get troubled individuals to the point where they can live independently, including clearing makeshift camps and using the threat of criminal punishment to get people to accept help from social services. Homeless advocates see things differently, favoring programs that aim at getting people shelter first and then using that as a stable base for them to receive additional services. They credit the 2026 decline to the same local programs and permanent housing policies the Trump administration wants to cut . The NAEH said that while there are many reasons for the drop, it’s “abundantly clear” that “homeless services systems and providers nationwide are successfully using their limited resources to reach people in need.” The advocates also point to veteran homelessness, which has fallen by nearly 60 percent since 2010 under the “Housing First” model , including another 7.8 percent this year as evidence their approach yields sustainable results if properly funded. Ann Oliva, the CEO of the National Alliance to End Homelessness, noted the administration hasn’t significantly changed its approach to veterans “because it’s been working.” She also told me the national decline was “quite broad based,” showing up in cities that sheltered large numbers of migrants as well as in places that didn’t. The debate over what’s driving the decline comes as lawmakers, advocates, and the courts fight over the future of homelessness policy — and which competing programs limited pools of funding should go toward. In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that cities can punish people for sleeping outside even when there aren’t enough shelter beds for them, and hundreds of cities and more than a dozen states have since passed or stepped up enforcing camping bans. Since taking office, President Donald Trump has gone further, attacking Housing First policies and trying to steer federal homelessness money away from permanent housing and toward short-term housing and treatment programs. His administration has repeatedly lost in court, most recently last week, when a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down HUD’s plan to set aside $1.3 billion of this year’s roughly $4 billion in homeless grants for short-term programs. The ruling means programs that already provide permanent housing can compete for that money again, and HUD has until the end of the year to distribute the funds. All the back-and-forth has been hard on the people running these programs. In a survey by NAEH, nearly half of local homelessness leaders said the uncertainty over federal money had already led programs in their area to cut services or shut them down. Why is chronic homelessness stuck? Chronically homeless people are often the hardest to move into permanent, stable housing. Most are poor and have a serious mental illness or addiction, and many have criminal records that make landlords balk at renting to them. And if they do manage to find a place to live, they often need ongoing supportive services to keep it. Their numbers hit a record high in HUD’s 2025 report, at 155,750 people nationwide, with over 40 percent of them living in California . HUD didn’t release a preliminary figure for chronic homelessness this month, but NAEH estimates it rose about 1 percent in 2026 . Their estimate’s margin of error includes a small decline, so it’s not yet clear whether chronic homelessness changed at all this year. Oliva, NAEH’s CEO, argues that a big part of why chronic homelessness is stuck is that communities don’t have enough housing. Her organization estimates there was enough permanent housing for only about 9 percent of people who were homeless during the 2025 count. She agrees with the Trump administration that more mental health and addiction services are needed, but she pointed to the administration’s cuts to Medicaid , which is the main way many homeless people access that care. Cutting Medicaid while asking HUD’s homelessness program to fill the gap, she told me, is “backwards from a public policy perspective.” And the longer people wait for housing, the harder they become to help. “People are aging into chronicity,” Oliva said. The Trump administration has been arguing that giving people housing without mandating treatment leaves too many problems unaddressed, and that being housed without improvements in health or substance use doesn’t actually represent real progress. Critics of Housing First point to studies that found limited evidence of improved health outcomes among Housing First participants . But proponents of it point to other rigorous research demonstrating its success in stably housing individuals , and say the voluntary approach to services helps preserve client dignity and autonomy while increasing the odds that people actually embrace and stick with treatment. Devon Kurtz, the director of public safety policy at the Cicero Institute, a conservative think tank that has harshly criticized Housing First and pushed for stricter enforcement of camping bans, told me he isn’t actually against Housing First. “It’s that requiring the system to have a one-size-fits-all housing-first model hasn’t worked,” he said. Kurtz wants communities to be able to use Housing First for some people while requiring others to get treatment, and he sees tougher enforcement as the main way to make that happen. “The criminal justice system is the lever by which we can get treatment first,” he said. Does tougher enforcement work? Plenty of cities aren’t waiting for HUD. After the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling, more than 350 cities and 14 states have passed laws or measures criminalizing homelessness , according to the National Homelessness Law Center. Kurtz pointed to Salt Lake City as an example of what that can look like. In a September op-ed in the Deseret News, he wrote that street homelessness in Salt Lake County fell 20 percent after the city began enforcing its camping ban , and that the county roughly doubled its open shelter beds over the same period. Kurtz acknowledges the numbers don’t prove the crackdown caused the drop, since Salt Lake also added shelter beds and passed a law making it easier to hold people in jail. And fewer people on the street doesn’t mean more people with homes. But even with those caveats, Kurtz said Salt Lake shows tougher enforcement doesn’t make homelessness worse, as critics often warn. Adam Ruege, the principal of policy and evaluation at the nonprofit Community Solutions, sees it differently. In places that lead with enforcement, he told me, “It creates a cycle of jail stays . They come back out on the street and have nowhere to go, and ultimately it costs communities more.” When I asked Kurtz for the strongest evidence that moving federal money away from permanent housing would work better, he named San Jose, California; San Francisco; Denver; and Salt Lake City. All four have seen significant drops in the number of people sleeping outside, while opening more shelter beds and, in most cases, stepping up enforcement of camping rules. But Kurtz himself described those cities as building on their existing systems, not replacing them. “They are merging the approaches,” he said. “They are still maintaining a substantial part of the existing [Housing First] system.” That’s a far more moderate take than HUD’s, which declared this year that Housing First “ has been a profound failure by any measure .” All of this is coming to a head in the next few weeks. Congress gave HUD until December 1 to hand out the first round of this year’s roughly $4 billion in homelessness grants. Under last week’s ruling, the rest has to go out by the end of the year, though the administration could still appeal. Ruege told me those with the most to lose are the ones who already have a home. “This is not some conceptual ‘Housing First, Treatment First’ debate,” he said. “These changes will mostly affect people who are currently housed.”

items.originalTitle: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.author: Chantelle Lee
items.title: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.summary: Voting booths at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Nov. 1, 2026. —Emily Elconin—Bloomberg/Getty Images Republicans and Democrats in several states engaged in a bitter fight to redraw congressional maps in their parties’ favor leading up to this year’s midterms. But in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept across the country, that conflict may be dying down—at least for now. Typically, maps are redrawn after the results of the U.S. census are released each decade, in order to account for population and demographic changes. Last year, however, President Donald Trump urged members of his party to redistrict mid-cycle ahead of the 2026 election as the GOP vied to hold onto its narrow House majority. Several Republican-led states moved to do so in the ensuing months, while Democratic leaders in other states responded with their own redistricting efforts, with varying degrees of success. The sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, though, could mark a shift in the redistricting battle, political experts tell TIME. Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding? Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that Republicans may be more reluctant to push for redistricting mid-cycle going forward, given that their efforts failed to counteract the blue wave in this year’s election . In states like Texas , North Carolina, Ohio , Alabama, and Florida , Democratic candidates came out on top in multiple districts that had been redrawn to benefit Republicans—which political experts have largely attributed to the fact that, despite redistricting efforts, Republicans were still facing a challenging political climate at a time when Trump’s approval rating was at a historic low . “In recent years, Democrats have been reluctant to engage in mid-cycle redistricting. Republicans have been more willing to do that, and Democrats have followed suit in response in order to counteract some of the districts created by Republicans to advantage themselves,” Panagopoulos says. “But as 2026 showed us, those efforts often amount to very little and can even backfire, so I think both parties right now are cautious about any mid-cycle redistricting efforts, and 2026 suggests that even if districts are very heavily gerrymandered to advantage one party or the other, there are no guarantees that those parties will win,” he continues. Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University, says that, for Republicans, “pretty much anything that they could have done, they already did.” And he says that even if there are states where additional redistricting could in theory help make maps even more favorable for Republicans, GOP lawmakers will now face a challenging time pushing such legislation through if their power in the state governments was reduced—for instance, in Texas, where Democrats gained control of the state House and the governorship . Meanwhile, the Democrats who were advocating for redistricting in recent months were doing so as “defensive measures,” says Alvin Tillery, the director of Northwestern University’s Center for the Study of Democratic Governance and a Democratic pollster and consultant. And Jones says that, with the party’s sizable victories in this year’s midterms, “the sense of urgency” to redistrict “is no longer there.” It’s possible, Jones says, that some “unfinished business” may continue — for instance, Virginians passed a redistricting ballot measure in April, but the state Supreme Court prevented the newly drawn maps from taking effect; Jones says that Democrats could try to take up that effort again. But generally speaking, “I don’t think we’re going to see the gerrymander armed race in 2027 that we saw in 2025,” Jones says. If some of those efforts do proceed, he says, “I think it’s going to be at the margins.” “The Democratic Party reluctantly engaged in mid-decade redistricting only after Donald Trump and Republicans drew first blood, and given the size of the victory and the lesser the sense of urgency and need to bolster the number of seats that are safely Democratic, I think we’re going to see Democrats try to return to the norms that have governed U.S. politics in the modern era,” Jones says. That doesn’t mean that partisan gerrymandering has come to an end, experts point out. The next redistricting cycle will take place after the 2030 census, and Panagopoulos says, “When it’s a redistricting cycle, both parties engage to the extent that they can in partisan gerrymandering.” And Democrats, he says, “will remain better positioned to engage in pro-Democratic redistricting in part because of the gains that they made in state legislatures and governorships across the country.” “I don’t think redistricting is high on any party’s agenda at the moment,” Panagopoulos says. But, he continues, “Things will clearly shift in the aftermath of the 2030 survey, and what will be more important is what the partisan makeup of states and state legislatures looks like at that time.”

items.originalTitle: ‘They’ll all go to Florida’: New IRS data reignites the fight over Massachusetts’ millionaires tax
items.author: Emma Witman
items.title: ‘They’ll all go to Florida’: New IRS data reignites the fight over Massachusetts’ millionaires tax
items.summary: New IRS figures may offer the clearest picture yet of how Massachusetts’ surtax on high-income residents is shaping the state’s population—and the tax base the ballot measure sought to tap. Massachusetts lost a net 31,384 residents to other states and countries between 2023 and 2024, according to IRS data reported by Boston.com . Those departing households took $3.64 billion in adjusted gross income with them. The net migration loss was slightly larger than the year before, though the income loss shrank from $4.18 billion. The numbers arrive nearly four years after the so-called “millionaires tax”—a 4% surcharge on annual income above roughly $1.1 million, indexed to inflation—took effect to fund schools and transportation. The figures capture moves, not their motives . Still, they are fuel for a perpetual debate: Do taxes on high earners drive wealthy households away, undermining the revenue they were meant to raise? New Hampshire and Florida absorb the biggest share Departing residents have clear destinations. New Hampshire gained a net 7,818 residents from Massachusetts, while Florida picked up 6,032. Together, those two states accounted for roughly 44% of Massachusetts’ net migration loss. The money followed the same routes. Massachusetts lost a net $1.29 billion in adjusted gross income to Florida and $869 million to New Hampshire, together about 59% of the state’s total. Neither destination has a state income tax. Each of Massachusetts’ New England neighbors—New Hampshire, Maine, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Vermont—also gained more residents from the Bay State than it sent back. Young professionals and high earners drove much of the loss, according to an analysis of the IRS data by the Pioneer Institute, a Boston-based think tank. Tax filers ages 26 to 34 made up 43% of the state’s net loss of filers in 2024, and those earning $200,000 or more accounted for $2.32 billion, or 64%, of the net income loss. The IRS tracks migration by comparing addresses on consecutive years’ tax returns, capturing both the number of people on those returns and their adjusted gross income. The traffic ran both ways. New York sent the most newcomers to Massachusetts (13,394), followed by Florida (11,728) and California (8,728). Massachusetts also led its exchanges with a handful of states, with a net gain of 855 residents from New Jersey, plus smaller gains from Louisiana and Indiana. The surtax keeps beating its forecasts Whatever the migration data show, the tax itself has not come up short. The Massachusetts Department of Revenue preliminarily certified $3.38 billion in surtax collections for fiscal 2026 , a record, and well above the $2.4 billion the state budget had assumed . That compares with roughly $3 billion in fiscal 2025 and the $1.8 billion the state reported in May 2024, double what officials expected . Supporters and critics read the same numbers differently. After the IRS’s March release, MassBudget, a Boston-based research group, argued the data showed affordability, not taxes, driving the state’s out-migration . Other states are moving in Massachusetts’ direction regardless. Washington voters on Nov. 3 kept a new 9.9% tax on income above $1 million, and two of the neighbors now gaining Bay Staters, Maine and Rhode Island, enacted their own surcharges on millionaire income this year . An income tax is not a wealth tax The Massachusetts data lands amid a broader debate over whether governments can tax high earners and wealthy households without prompting them to move. But the policies under scrutiny aren’t all the same. Massachusetts’ millionaires tax is an income tax surcharge: It adds 4 percentage points to the state income tax on annual income above the threshold. California’s Proposition 40, which voters rejected on Nov. 3, targeted wealth itself, with a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. A wealth tax can apply even when assets are “unrealized,” meaning they haven’t been sold or generated taxable income. Peter Barnes, a former U.S. deputy international tax counsel and longtime General Electric tax lawyer, said the history of wealth taxes abroad warns states attempting them on their own. He noted that France saw flight from its wealth tax and has since effectively eliminated it, replacing it in 2018 with a narrower levy on real estate. “That’s the same thing that doomed the California wealth tax—this idea that, ‘Oh my god, they’ll all go to Florida,’” Barnes said. “I think first of all, it needs to be a whole U.S. federal tax. I don’t think a state can successfully do it.” Chester Spatt, a professor of finance at Carnegie Mellon University, previously told Fortune he was skeptical that steep wealth taxes can generate the revenue their proponents expect. “It would indirectly represent a very heavy tax on investment income,” Spatt said. “I suspect it won’t raise much revenue and instead lead to the development of devices that would be outside the reach of the tax.” For now, Massachusetts remains a laboratory of democracy—testing whether taxing high earners at the state level can work, or whether, as critics warn, it simply accelerates their departure. items.originalTitle: A study of 22,894 Oura Ring wearers ties erratic sleep times to depression and anxiety. Its author offers a simple solution
items.author: Lara Murray-Sterzel
items.title: A study of 22,894 Oura Ring wearers ties erratic sleep times to depression and anxiety. Its author offers a simple solution
items.summary: How long you sleep is only part of the picture. In a study of 22,894 adults who wore Oura smart rings for an average of 154 days, people whose bedtimes and wake times shifted from day to day reported more severe depression, anxiety, and loneliness, and the link held after researchers accounted for how long people slept. The research, led by UC San Francisco and UC San Diego and published Nov. 12 in Scientific Reports , measured consistency with the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) , a 0-to-100 score. A score of 100 means someone falls asleep and wakes up at identical times every day; lower scores mean more drift. Sleep trouble is common. In 2020, 14.5% of U.S. adults had trouble falling asleep most days or every day, and 17.8% had trouble staying asleep, according to the CDC. Most advice for them centers on duration and habits, from the best sleeping position to a consistent bedtime routine . The findings also come as sleep tracking turns into big business. Oura, whose rings supplied the data and which helped fund the study, put its planned IPO on hold this fall ; at the top of its proposed range, the offering would have valued the company at $15.6 billion. Why months of data beat a single week Participants took part in TemPredict, a study launched in 2020 that used smart-ring sleep and movement data synced to the Oura app. They also completed monthly surveys on depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Researchers compared the full multi-month record against a seven-day “Typical Week” snapshot, the window most earlier sleep-regularity studies relied on. Both approaches pointed the same way, but the longer data showed stronger links to mental health. An irregular sleeper’s single week might happen to catch an unusually steady stretch. “We capture the ups and the downs, the harder weeks and the easier weeks, and we obtain a more complete picture of what someone’s sleep looks like over time,” said Ashley Mason, the study’s senior author and an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF. “Short-term tracking may underestimate—but may overestimate—irregular sleep, depending on when you capture it.” Longer tracking, Mason said, can “minimize the impact that unrepresentative weeks have on a dataset.” She pointed to a UK Biobank analysis of nearly 80,000 participants that relied on one week of wrist-worn sleep data. Shyamal Patel, Oura’s senior vice president of science, said the signal from longer tracking was stronger than in a “typical week” snapshot, “which is how much shorter past studies measured sleep regularity. That’s exactly how Oura can support researchers–by making sleep-wake patterns measurable in everyday life over time, especially when paired with repeated assessments of mood and symptoms. Then, randomized interventions can test whether changing sleep routines changes outcomes.” What the numbers show According to first author Severine Soltani, an SRI of 84 corresponds to going to bed and waking up roughly an hour earlier or later than the day before, on average. At 75, that shift is closer to an hour and a half. Scores tracked symptom severity. Participants with severe depression averaged an SRI of 74.93, compared with 83.74 for those within normal limits. For severe anxiety, the average was 78.94, versus 83.67. Each 5-point drop in SRI was associated with roughly 1.5 times higher odds of severe depression. That association held after the researchers adjusted for age, sex, and average sleep duration. Mason calls the findings “correlational in nature.” She pointed to a JAMA Psychiatry study published in February, which found that irregular sleep predicted depressive relapse among adults in remission, as evidence that prioritizing regular sleep may lower the risk of declining mental health. “Sleep irregularity most likely harms mental health through circadian misalignment and its downstream effects—on hormones, inflammation, neurotransmitters, emotion regulation, and our social lives,” Mason said. “When we support circadian rhythms, we support other bodily functions.” The loneliness link Participants who reported elevated loneliness averaged an SRI of 81.79, compared with 83.75 for those within normal limits. The authors noted that sleep-regularity research has paid little attention to loneliness, despite its toll on mental health. Mason said her team approached loneliness with an “exploratory mindset” because the connection “hasn’t been studied before.” The result made sense to her once she thought about everyday routines. “If you have a morning workout class that you always go to and see friends at, you are more likely to have a regular time you wake up in order to get to the class,” she said. “Sleep regularity may be associated with other types of schedule regularity that involve social interactions.” Who funded the study, and what it can’t prove The analysis is cross-sectional, and symptoms were self-reported, so it can’t show that irregular sleep causes depression or the reverse. The study notes that participants were disproportionately white, middle-aged, and living in North America and Europe. Because the study began during the COVID-19 pandemic, the researchers focused on main sleep episodes, excluded shift workers, and did not control for factors such as living alone or individual chronotypes. Funding came from the U.S. Department of Defense, the #StartSmall Foundation, and Oura Health Oy. Mason has been paid for consulting work for Oura, and co-author Benjamin Smarr of UC San Diego has been paid for consulting work and holds a financial interest in the company. What to do with it Asked whether Oura plans to turn SRI into real-time guidance, Patel pointed to features the company already offers: Bedtime Guidance and Chronotype , “which together evaluate a user’s circadian rhythm, and provide a personalized bedtime window that appears an hour before it begins.” A Body Clock graph compares members’ recent sleep with their optimal window. Patel said Oura focuses on “giving members perspective rather than fueling fixation.” “We don’t think perfect sleep is the goal. A consistent routine that fits someone’s life is more realistic and easier to keep up,” he said. “We want members to understand their bodies with more confidence, so they can live their fullest and most vibrant life, not spend their time chasing scores.” Mason’s advice requires no device. “We cannot wave a magic wand and make ourselves fall asleep at the same time every day, but we can set an alarm clock and make ourselves wake up at the same time every day,” she said. “If you wake up at the same time every day that ends in D-A-Y (Monday, Saturday, Sunday, Tuesday, and so on), you will start to get sleepy at the same time each night, and your bedtime will regularize.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.title: ‘If the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?’ Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
items.summary: Brands know use of agents such as Meta Muse is on the rise but are unlikely to hand them the keys to the shop They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.
